The Americau Rifemen The contest for the Leech Cup on Saturday (says the N.Y.Herald) tried the mettieofour riflemen,and the work they did showed clear- ly that the honor of the country may be safely left in their keeping.The scores made by the principal members of the team have sel- dom been surpassed and perhaps have never been equalled i the aggregate by four mem bers of any team. Colonel Bodine,whose skill and nerve secured victory for America, won the Leech Cup with one of the highes scores on reecrd. Messrs. Fulton, Gilder- sleeve and Coleman pressed him very closely, and it may be said to have been a neck-and neck race betiveen the latter gentleman fo the second plice.Mr. Coleman's score is especially honorable, because it was the first
time he ever shot on the new target. We append a few of the higher scores: Col. Jobn Bodin... 205 Col.H.A. Gildeisleeve. 193 Major Henry Fton 198 R.C.Coleman 195 191 L.L.Hepburn... 177 A.V.Canfield,J. Capt.L.C.Brucs. 176 176 H.s.Hewel..... The New York Herald says: The day was clear, bright and warm,the wind gentle, and
blowing up the range in a direction almost parallel to the line of fire. The match i the first that has come off in this country at the new target lately adopted from the Wimbledon model,which prescribes a circular,instead of a square bulls ee. As will be seen from the scores published below the records of yesterday's shooting are far ahead of anything that has ever been done in front of the old square bulls.eye. What was lone yesterday may now be compared with scores made by the Irish riflemen at their late practices in Dublinand Belfast. It is already on record that in Ireland 208,203 and 202 have been made at the new targets, Mr. McKenna,of Belfast, having been eredited with the highest of the scores mentioned above. The highest score yet made in Ainerica before a long range tar- get was achieved yesterday by Colonel Bo dine, who won the Leech Cup on a record of 205 out of a possible 225..It will bere- membered that the other dayColonel Bo- dine made 162 points out of a possible 180, the highest aggregate attained this season at any of the contests for places on the American Team or the subsequent practices of this team. These records place Colonel o pe n e or Fulton, and at any rate his victory yester- day puts him for the coming year at the head of American riflemen and confirms his right to the titleofOldReliable,withwhich riflemen have saluted him. Only meagre reports of the practice in Ire- land have reached this side of the Atlantic; but,without going into tiresome details of figures,it is sale to state that there is hardly the flip of a copper's difference in choice between the two international teams.

Sir Hleury Thompson on Vivisection. (London Morning Advertiser,May 18th.) Sir Henry Thompson's opinions upon surgical, and doubtless upon many other
matters, are entitled to be received with re- spect. But the most learned men and the most skilful operatora are not infallible on all subjects. Thus Sir Henry in his partial de- fence of the demoniacl practice of vivisection as at present conducted, has contrved to write a little just a very littleabsolutenon- sense ; and we not only take the liberty to tell him so, but shall proceed to prove it. Sir Henry Thompson endeavors to show that there are many customs annually in use amongst us far more cruel than vivisection, and less defensible. Now,here we join issue with him.-We have not a word to sayin de- fence of those disgusting and cruel fy-papers
vulgarly calledcatch-em-alive ohs.We confess that we cannot endure to see them, and would never tolerate their use Probably the addition of a little poison to theglutinous composition with which these abominable sheets of insect torture are smeared wouldre- move the objection.But does Sir Henry Thompson pretend to say that a fy feelsthe same pain as one of the higher order of ani- mals-say,for instance,a dog?If a dog's leg is torn offcan he run merrily away and
feed?But if a fly chance to lose a leg,it will not prevent him from sitting on a lumpof sugar a minute after: tear a leg inthe same manner from a man, and in all probability he dies.Again,would Sir Henry Thompson compare smoking a waspsnest to the destruction of human life in the caves of Dahra? Sir Henry cites the cruelty of the angler. Now,a fish is far higher in the sale of creation than a maggot or a worm. But he tells us that worms on the fisherman's
hook suffer more than the dogs in the vivi- sector's operating-roomfaithful creatures whose agonies have been so graphically de scribed by a medioal man,that it is difficult to banish the hideous picture from the mind. Now,with regard to a fish, we ask if adog,
much more a human being, were to get a fight of hooks of proportionate size to those which are used to capture fish-of let us say some three or four pounds weight,would that dog,after being dragged about for a quarter of an hour or so by these hooks fixed to a cord,should he happen then to escape with his throat and jaws torn,mangled and bleed ing,rush at and greedily devour a piece of meat upon another similar flight of hooks,or a e e p cisely what a fish will do. Even in flv-fish-
ing many an angler has recovered his hook in the mouth of a salmon,trout,or grayling, lost,it may be,half an hour before,the fish rising again to the lure.Apike has been known during the last season to be hookedby two anglers one after the otherand has thus been captured, as a joint possession, by both. There never was,in our opinion,a more mis- taken notion than that so charmingly con- veyedby Shakspere in the well-known pas- sage- "The poor beetle that we tread upon In corporal sufferance foels a pang as great And when a giant dies."

In the interval between the adjournment of the Court yesterday evening and the meeting this morning,I carefully read and considered the whole evidence. The result at which I arrived i regard to the acts of the repond ent and others on the polling dayand during the hours appointed for taking the polls at Davidson's Hotelin the village of Carlisle, rendered it unnecessary in my opinion to de- termine any other of the charges advanced for the purpose of avoiding the election. My finding and my report to the Speaker willbe limited to that one matter. It will be convenient to begin by referring to the statutory provisions on which this charge of corrupt practices is founded. They are contained in the Ontario statutes, 32 Vic.ch.21sec.66:36 Vie.,ch.2,sec.1 and sec.3.sub-sec.l and 2. The first of these enactments is,"Every hotel, tavern,and shop in which spiriuous or fermented liquors or drinks are ordiarily sold shall be closed during the day appointed for polling in the wards or municipalities in which the polls are held; and no spirituous or fermented liquors or drinks shall be sold or given to any person within the limits of such municipality during the said period, under a penalty of $1oo,in every suchr case. 2nd. "Corrupt practices or corrupt practice' shall mean bribery,treating, and undue inf nence, or any of sueh offences as defined by this or any act of the Legislature, or recognized by the Common Law of the Parliament of England；alsoany violation of the 46th,61st,or 7lst sections of the Elee- tion Law of 1868; and any violation of the 66th section of such last mentioned Act dur- ing the hours appointed for polling. 3rd:"When it is found upon the report of a judge upon an election petition that any corrupt practice has been committed by any candidate atan election, or by his agent, whether with or without the actual know- ledge and consent of such candidate, the election of such candidate, if he has been elected, shall be void." And further, when it has in like manner been found that any corrupt practice has been committed by or with the actual knowledge or (query,if this should not be and) consent of any candidate at an election in addition to his election,if he has been electedbeing void, he shall during the eight years next after the date of ea go eq e p o u n ing elected," &c., &c. LIGHTHOUSE ILLUMINATION.-The nECeSSity of intense illumination for lighthouses has induced the English Government to undertake various experiments with a view to realize this object.At one of their coast stations there are employed for this purpose two magneto-electric machines, each being put in motion by a two-horse power steam engine, and, excepting.wear and tear, the whole consumption of material to produce the light is the coke andwater required to raise steam for the engine and carbonpoints for the lamp in the lantern.The lamp is a delicate arrangement of machinery,holding the two carbons between which the electric light exists,and regulating their adjustment, so that while they gradually consume away the place of the light shall not bealtered.The electrie wires end in thetwo bars of a small railway, and upon these the lamp stands. When the carbons of a lamp are nearly gone that lamp is lifted off and another instantly pushed into its place.The light never goes out through any deficiency or cause in the engine and machine house,and when ithas become extinguished in the lantern a single touch of the keeper's hand sets it shining as bright as ever,sending forth its illumination with a power of brilliancy far surpassipg that of any other fixed light.
